books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Southern Chivalry — Argument versus Club’s (John L. Magee, 1856)

stimulus.source_note: Southern Chivalry — Argument versus Club’s (John L. Magee, lithograph, 1856). Smithsonian, National Museum of American History (nmah_325684); Wikimedia Commons, File:Southern_Chivalry.jpg. Public domain.
stimulus.text: A lithograph published in 1856, titled “Southern Chivalry — Argument versus Club’s.” It shows Representative Preston Brooks of South Carolina standing over Senator Charles Sumner of Massachusetts, who has fallen from his chair on the Senate floor, bleeding from the head and still holding a quill. Brooks raises his cane for another blow. In Sumner’s other hand is a paper marked “KANSAS.” Other members of Congress watch from behind, some smiling, some reaching out to stop the fight.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: Northern and Southern reactions to the beating best illustrate that by 1856

options.text: Congress had agreed to admit Kansas as a free state.
options.misconception: Background from the books: Congress did not admit Kansas until January 1861, as a free state; the beating settled nothing.

options.text: the new Republican Party had already won the presidency.
options.misconception: Background from the books: the Republicans would not win the presidency until Lincoln in 1860; Frémont lost in 1856.

rationales.A: Background from the books: Congress did not admit Kansas until January 1861, as a free state; the beating settled nothing.
rationales.B: Background from the books: the Republicans would not win the presidency until Lincoln in 1860; Frémont lost in 1856.
rationales.C: Background from the books: Northerners saw a martyr and Southerners saw a hero, and each side praised its own man.
rationales.D: Background from the books: the Court’s Dred Scott ruling came in 1857 and deepened the quarrel; it settled nothing.
rationales.general:
1. Watch the North: Sumner became a martyr, proof of Southern barbarity.
2. Watch the South: Brooks became a hero, praised for defending Southern honor.
3. See the split: one beating, two opposite stories, and no shared facts left.
4. Note the timing: the beating came the day after the Sack of Lawrence, so the North read it as one assault.
Remember: when two sides cheer opposite heroes for one event, the Union is already coming apart.
